summary:
Yobe State stands under the national framework of Nigeria. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies nationwide and reaches well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests.

Sexual orientation and gender identity carry criminal exposure at entry. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (Version 4.0, June 2025, updated April 2026) records that same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that Sharia law in all twelve northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.

Yobe is one of the twelve states that adopted Sharia into criminal legislation by 2002, the only states whose Sharia courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law, according to Human Rights Watch's 2004 report. Sharia was established in Yobe in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim, and the state's inhabitants are mainly Muslims, which is how Yobe acquired a parallel religious-criminal jurisdiction for Muslims during the 1999-2002 wave.

For a trans visitor this makes Yobe a jurisdiction-level rather than incident-level risk. The same UK Home Office note (June 2025) states that the federal criminal code penalises same-sex male conduct with up to 14 years' imprisonment and three years for attempts while being silent on women, that the Sharia penal codes of the twelve states apply to Muslims, and that death is the maximum penalty for men in all twelve of them. Penalties for acts between women range from death in a minority of states to flogging and imprisonment. The note's enforcement and Hisbah section records the public flogging in 2023 of a person for cross-dressing, and observes that few secular cases reach court.

Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

Trans people in Nigeria face documented killing and official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing, and the Abuja police chief ordered a thorough and discreet investigation. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against perceived gay people is a routine feature of enforcement. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old man stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Visitors who use dating apps face entrapment: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The only trans-specific imprisonment case in these sources concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, which she served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
The twelve-state pattern is a legal architecture rather than a scattering of local incidents. Human Rights Watch's 2004 reporting describes a defined group of states whose Sharia courts try Muslim criminal cases beyond federal law, which is why Yobe's exposure is structural: the jurisdiction itself supplies the penalty, not a single enforcement campaign.

The federal and religious layers differ in how they treat women. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records that the federal criminal code is silent on same-sex conduct between women, while the state Sharia penal codes reach it with penalties that vary from state to state, including death in a minority of jurisdictions. A trans woman or lesbian therefore faces two different bodies of law depending on whether she is treated as a Muslim defendant in a state religious court or as a defendant under the national criminal code.

Enforcement in practice does not track the statutory text closely. The same note observes that few secular cases reach court, while religious-police punishment can be administered publicly and extrajudicially, as with the 2023 flogging for cross-dressing. The pattern documented in Lagos, where a man was beaten and extorted for appearing gay, suggests that the SSMPA functions as leverage for police bribery independent of prosecution.

Yobe's majority-Muslim population and its adoption of Sharia in 2000 under Governor Bukar Abba Ibrahim place it within the same wave as the other eleven states, rather than marking it as an outlier with unusually aggressive local practice.
localsOnly:
Residents who are Muslim in Yobe State are subject to the state's religious penal code in addition to national law, and the religious courts have jurisdiction over their criminal cases. Non-Muslim residents fall under the federal and state secular criminal code, under which same-sex male conduct carries up to 14 years' imprisonment and attempts three years.

For Muslim men, death is the maximum penalty for same-sex acts under Yobe's Zina provisions, as it is across all twelve states with Sharia criminal jurisdiction. For women, the applicable penalty depends on the specific state code, ranging from death in a minority of the twelve states to flogging and imprisonment.

Hisbah religious police operate as an enforcement channel, and the UK Home Office records public flogging as a punishment actually imposed for cross-dressing in 2023. Few secular cases reach the courts, so exposure for residents more commonly arises through religious-police action, community denunciation or police extortion than through formal prosecution.

Imprisonment conditions for trans detainees are set by administrative discretion. In the Bobrisky case the authorities placed a transgender woman in a maximum-security prison, and press coverage at the time openly debated which prison would hold her, indicating that housing between male and female sections was not governed by a published rule. An October 2024 investigative panel found that the placement violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender, but the panel addressed the security classification rather than gender placement.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here, and the same applies to Yobe specifically.

The sources do not resolve whether a foreign national visiting Yobe would be tried in a state Sharia court or under the federal criminal code, nor whether religious-law jurisdiction turns on self-identification, residence or any other test. The June 2025 Home Office note states that the Sharia penal codes apply to Muslims without setting out how that status is determined for visitors.

Which specific penalty for same-sex conduct between women applies in Yobe is not stated: the Home Office note gives a range across the twelve states, and the sources gathered here do not identify Yobe's own provision within that range.

The current text of Yobe's own penal code, including any express provision on cross-dressing or gender expression, is not sourced here; the cross-dressing enforcement recorded for 2023 is documented without a named state, so its attribution to Yobe is unresolved.

No incident of a trans visitor being prosecuted, killed or assaulted in Yobe is documented in these sources, so the state-level assessment rests on the legal framework and the national record rather than on Yobe-specific case evidence.
